title: Gulliver's in Paterson and talk with Art Vincent and Al Pryor
summary: Her Newark radio appearance, the Paterson club, and a conversation about musicians' plight and neglected recordings.

blocks.x: Something else that was memorable to me from last Thursday out there in Newark, was that lunch time conversation we had with Art Vincent --
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Oh yeah.
Your host on the show. You want to say why you were appearing on that show?

Yeah. I went out to do an interview with Art Vincent, because during the time that I was in the hospital, Art had announced it on the radio. And I got a lot of letters of condolence from his having announced this. And so in the meantime, he called me when I got home and wanted to know if I'd come out. Well I had done an interview with Art some years ago. And he remembered that. I supposed he was a little reluctant to ask me to come all the way out to Newark to do an interview, but I was glad to get out there. And one of the reasons why I was glad to get our there, because The House That Jazz Built was having their annual meeting. And Amos and Pat Kaune who own Gulliver's, are sponsoring a benefit for The House That Jazz Built on Wednesday, July 23rd.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Gulliver's, we should say for the people way ahead in the future will be listening to this or reading this, is a music spot in Patterson, New Jersey.
Right. It's one of the few places where the artist really likes to work, because the manager is a jazz lover.
We got into a very stimulating conversation after the interview in the restaurant there with Art and Al Pryor.

Okay, you were saying about Al Pryor.

Yeah. I was quite fascinated by Al's conversation. As I remarked later, Al sort of represents the new breed of music critic, I might say. And he's sort of wrapped up in the protest against what happened to musicians in the past. And we had a very difficult time trying to convince Al that those were different times. He became especially concerned over the fact that I had recorded "Loch Lomond" for twenty-five dollars. "See that, that's what I mean." Now, you know that's my right. And, of course, I told him at that time I would've paid them to make the recording. And he is quite concerned and wants to do quite a few more of these things that have to do
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
with the status of musicians and their plight with their industry.
He's concerned about the fact that a lot of good music was recorded, and the musicians not only didn't get credit for it, they're not included in the residuals.
